summary: Illinois requires working smoke alarms and CO alarms in every home all the time, not just at sale - selling does not trigger any extra step, but a buyer's new home has to meet the same rules the seller did.
alarmType: At least one approved smoke detector, in operating condition, within 15 feet of every room used for sleeping, mounted on the ceiling at least 6 inches from a wall or on a wall 4 to 6 inches below the ceiling. A single-family home also needs one on every story including the basement, but not an unoccupied attic. An 'approved' detector is an ionization or photoelectric unit meeting Illinois State Fire Marshal rules. In a home that existed on July 1, 1988, alarms may be battery powered - but the battery must be a self-contained, non-removable, long-term battery (the sealed 10-year type) - or wired to the house AC, and they need not be interconnected. That sealed-battery rule bites on any battery alarm more than 10 years past its manufacture date, any that fails a test or malfunctions, and any newly installed one. It does not apply to alarms that are part of a centrally monitored or supervised system, or that use low-power radio frequency or Wi-Fi/wireless networking, or to other devices the State Fire Marshal exempts by rule. A home newly built, reconstructed or substantially remodeled after December 31, 1987 must have alarms permanently wired into the AC power line and, where more than one is required, interconnected so one sounding sets off all. For that work done on or after January 1, 2011, the hardwired alarms must also have back-up power (battery or emergency generator).
coAlarms: Separate act, and it is not tied to sale either. Every dwelling unit must have at least one approved CO alarm in operating condition within 15 feet of every room used for sleeping. It may be battery powered, plug-in with battery back-up, or wired to the house AC with secondary battery back-up, and may be a combination smoke/CO unit if the combined device meets both sets of rules and sounds the two hazards differently. An approved alarm must bear a nationally recognized testing laboratory label and meet current UL or CSA standards. Exempt: a unit in a building that does not burn fossil fuel for heat, ventilation or hot water, is not connected in any way to a garage, and is not close enough to a ventilated CO source (as the local building commissioner determines) to receive CO from it; and any unit the local building commissioner finds is not close enough to a CO source to be at risk. Cite: 430 ILCS 135/10, 135/20 (Carbon Monoxide Alarm Detector Act), https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/ILCS/Articles?ActID=2786&ChapterID=39 - enacted P.A. 94-741, effective January 1, 2007.
certification: Nobody inspects or certifies at sale. Enforcement is by penalty, not paperwork: willful failure to install or maintain a required smoke detector or CO alarm is a Class B misdemeanor, and tampering with or removing one (or its batteries) is a Class A misdemeanor, a Class 4 felony on a second conviction. For the sealed-battery rule specifically, the owner gets a 90-day warning to fix it, then fines up to $100 and another $100 every 30 days until fixed or until the fines total $1,500; if it is corrected by the hearing date the violation is dismissed.
citation: 425 ILCS 60/2, 60/3, 60/4 (Smoke Detector Act); 430 ILCS 135/5, 135/10, 135/15, 135/20 (Carbon Monoxide Alarm Detector Act)
